newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Rebel Albanian city gives cool welcome to king.
newsitem.headline: Rebel Albanian city gives cool welcome to king.

text.p: Albania's long-exiled King Leka received a lukewarm welcome on Thursday in the rebel-held southern city of Vlore from about 5,000 people who chanted slogans against President Sali Berisha.
Chants of "Down with Berisha" interrupted Leka's speech in the city square as he appealed for peace and unity to resolve the country's crisis.
Witnesses said Vlore residents, who gather daily at the square to attend rallies by the rebel committee that controls the city, were respectful to Leka but unenthusiastic.
"Peace, unity, cooperation and brotherhood. These are the words which should give life back to the country," said the bespectacled Leka, 58, speaking through a megaphone.
He laid a wreath for Ismail Qemali, who declared Albania's independence from the Ottoman Empire in 1912 and became its first Prime minister.

The people of Vlore have suffered more than most Albanians as nearly every family in the Adriatic port city invested their life savings in bogus investment schemes which have since collapsed. Most of the dubious savings plans were based in Vlore.
The collapse of the investment schemes triggered an armed insurrection in late February in which at least 300 people have been killed and more than 700 wounded.
Rebel committees blaming President Berisha, a northerner, for the collapse of the schemes have taken control of much of the south including Vlore.
No rebel committee leaders were on hand to welcome Leka, who has returned to Albania to press for peace and the restoration of the monarchy.
Vlore is not considered a bedrock of support for the monarchist cause. The king comes from northern Albania.
Last Sunday more than 5,000 people gave him a rousing welcome, firing rifles and pistols into the sky, at his ancestral village of Burgajet, north of the capital Tirana.
President Berisha has promised to hold a referendum on restoring the monarchy but has not set a date. Albania expects to hold general elections on June 29.
Leka believes he is the rightful leader of Albania based on a constitution adopted in 1928.
Leka was two days old when his father, King Zog, fled with his family in 1939 ahead of invading Italian troops. He returned home from exile in South Africa earlier this month.

In Tirana, central bank sources and newspapers said the supervising board of the Bank of Albania had chosen Qamil Tusha as the new governor and a presidential decree was expected to announce the appointment later.
Central bank sources told Reuters that Tusha, who was previously deputy director of the National Commercial Bank, a state-run commercial bank, had already taken up his duties.
Official spokesmen were not immediately available.
Newspapers said the outgoing governor, Kristaq Luniku, was now working with the International Monetary Fund in Washington advising on the Albanian economy, hard hit by the insurrection.
Prices of basic foodstuffs have soared in Europe's poorest country and the lek currency has dropped sharply against the U.S. dollar in recent months.
In the western port of Durres, more troops from an Italian-led multinational security force, which is deploying to protect humanitarian aid deliveries, continued to arrive.
About 300 Italian soldiers as well as tanks, armoured vehicles and trucks, landed by ferry, officials said.
Their arrival brings to 4,500 the total number of foreign troops now stationed in the country.
The force, which also includes soldiers from France, Spain, Greece, Turkey, Austria, Denmark and Romania, is expected to eventually number 6,000 men.
